Chapter 7: The University and the World—Systems, Conformity, and the Price of Originality.
As the miles roll by, the father’s thoughts drift back to another kind of journey—those years spent teaching at a university. You can almost picture the campus: part playground for big ideas, part battlefield where curiosity meets the pressures of fitting in.
He remembers the thrill when he first started out—how meaningful it felt to help students tackle life’s big questions. There was a purpose to those days, a sense that anything was possible. But as time passed, frustration crept in. The university, for all its talk about open minds and free thought, often seemed to reward sticking to the script instead of daring to be different. He watched new students, full of excitement, slowly learn how to play along—writing what professors wanted to hear, aiming for grades instead of real understanding.
One moment really stuck with him. There was this bright, curious student who just couldn’t pick a topic for her essay—nothing seemed meaningful enough. So, he suggested something simple: write about the front of a building she saw every day. At first, she pushed back, thinking it was way too ordinary. But when she actually started paying attention, really looking, she found layers of detail and meaning she’d never noticed before. That simple act of truly seeing—of engaging with what’s right in front of you—became the heart of her learning.
That experience made something crystal clear for him. Most systems—whether it’s school, work, or anything else—are built to create predictable outcomes. They want efficiency, order, control. But real learning and creativity? They come from being willing to see things differently, to question what everyone takes for granted, to risk being wrong. And honestly, originality often comes at a cost: misunderstanding, even rejection. The father’s own journey—as Phaedrus—was filled with clashes with colleagues, and a growing feeling that he just didn’t fit in as his ideas drifted further from the mainstream.
Out on the road, those memories take on a new life. He realizes the challenge isn’t just about resisting conformity. It’s about finding ways, every day, to keep creativity and curiosity alive. For Chris—for anyone trying to figure out this world—the lesson is simple but powerful: don’t be afraid to look closely, to ask your own questions, to trust what you see and feel. The systems around us might be strong, but they’re not the whole story. There’s always space for originality—for the quiet courage it takes to see things with fresh eyes.
